why.1: The output defines a lag stop at 1.40 m (proposed, adjustable, flagged OPEN). The setpoints are consistent: lead stop 0.6 < lag stop 1.4 < lead start 1.6 < lag start 2.0 < high alarm 2.3 < LSHH 2.6 < overflow 2.8. Setpoint validation rules enforce this ordering.
why.2: Section 8 specifies a hardwired float backup triggered by LSHH-121 that runs pumps at Preset Speed 2 without the PLC or LIT. It is powered from UPS 24 VDC, works with the PLC powered down, and is tested in FAT 19 and 23.
why.3: Section 5.2 detects failure from <3.6 or >21 mA for 5 s or a channel diagnostic. Section 5.3 adds float discrepancy checks. On failure the station raises an alarm, stops level-based control, and passes control to the float backup.
why.4: Section 7.5 covers fail-to-start (15 s with no running feedback), lost run feedback, VFD fault and motor protection trip. The output removes the command, latches and alarms, and promotes and immediately starts the other pump. FAT tests 11-13 cover this.
why.5: Section 10 and Section 14 specify a 10 s restart delay after ATS Emergency and Generator Running, or after PLC power-up. The lag starts at least 10 s after the lead, and the float backup uses a 10 s on-delay relay for VFD-122. FAT test 24 covers this.
why.6: Section 11.1 states the PLC operates autonomously and comm loss has no effect on pump control. Sections 6.2 and 9 state the hardwired LSL-121 interlock stops the pump in Hand, with a bypass question flagged OPEN. FAT test 17 tests this.

why.1: Section 5.4 sets a lag stop at 1.2 m. That is below lag start (2.0 m) and above lead stop (0.6 m). The setpoint table and ordering rule (LSL < stop < lead start < lag start < alarm < LSHH) place the 2.3 m alarm between lag start and LSHH, and the PLC rejects entries that break the ordering.
why.2: Section 5.6 has LSHH-121, a discrete float, command all available pumps to run at 60 Hz regardless of lead/lag logic. It is also described as wired to force pumps to run through the VFD. Section 6.1 has LSHH-121 call pumps when LIT-121 has failed. The action is triggered by the float, not the transducer, though the output leaves relay versus PLC implementation as a [CONFIRM] item.
why.3: Section 6.1 detects failure from signals below 3.5 mA or above 20.5 mA, frozen readings, and implausible jumps. Section 6.2 adds float/LIT disagreement checks. The response is a high-priority alarm, a switch to float-based backup control, and a defined return to normal control.
why.4: Section 5.5 says that if the lead pump fails to start or trips, the other pump is called immediately as lead, a fault alarm is raised, and the failed pump is locked out. Section 5.7 defines fail-to-run as no run feedback within 10 s. FAT tests 14 and 15 cover this.
why.5: Section 7 specifies a restart delay and staggered pump starts, at least 10 s apart, after generator transfer. The same sequence applies on retransfer to utility power, and FAT test 20 covers it.
why.6: Sections 4.2 and 9 state that loss of radio or SCADA does not affect local automatic control. Section 4.1 states that in HAND the LSL-121 low level cutout stays active as a hardwired protection, and FAT test 13 verifies it.

why.1: Section 2 says FAULT has no exit and must latch. The corrected model defines the reset as 'Cause cleared AND operator reset', entering OFF, or COOL-DOWN if hot. Restart always goes through PURGE.
why.2: Section 5 criticises the fixed 5-minute timer. It requires proven airflow and at least 4 volume changes, and says the purge timer must reset if any permissive is lost. The PURGE→IGNITION transition repeats this.
why.3: Section 4 says opening XV-601 from the faceplate bypasses the state logic. The operator should instead request PROCESS, and the sequence opens XV-601 only when permissives are met (flame, temperature, fan, LEL, valve positions).
why.4: Diversion is covered: below the permit minimum, close XV-601, open XV-602 and leave PROCESS. But the output never says to signal or alarm the coating line CL-6 on low temperature. It only loosely suggests 'consider interlocking CL-6' in the architecture section, which does not specify a signal when temperature falls below the destruction minimum.
why.5: Section 7 says the readiness setpoint must sit above the divert setpoint, otherwise the unit will cycle between READY and PROCESS at 760 °C. It also calls for a hold time and hysteresis (T_ready vs T_permit).
why.6: Fan behavior is defined: running in COOL-DOWN, and running in FAULT unless the fan caused the trip. But no Stop/shutdown transition is defined from PURGE or HEAT-UP. Stop is handled only from PROCESS (→READY) and READY (→COOL-DOWN).

why.1: Item 7 states FAULT has no exit and no reset path. Row 14 defines FAULT to PURGE on cause cleared plus operator acknowledge and reset, with cooling first if the chamber is hot.
why.2: Item 5 and row 2 say the purge timer runs only while airflow is proven and resets if airflow is lost.
why.3: Item 3 calls READY to PROCESS a bare HMI command and requires permissives enforced in logic, not just the faceplate. Row 4 makes fume admission a state-model sequence with permissives and position proving.
why.4: Item 1 flags that high fire alone is inadequate and an emissions exceedance. Row 7 closes XV-601, opens XV-602 and signals CL-6 to stop solvent when TT-601 stays below 760 C.
why.5: Item 11 states 760 C is both the entry and exit threshold, which chatters, and calls for a deadband with a delay. Rows 3, 5 and 7 apply the deadband and time delay.
why.6: Row 10 defines Stop from PURGE and HEAT-UP to COOL-DOWN (PURGE to OFF if cold). Item 15 and row 12 keep the fan running in COOL-DOWN until below 200 C. Item 7 and row 13 define fan behavior in FAULT: fan on for flame failure and over-temperature, and not stopped when the chamber is hot.

why.1: The conflicts table lists the HP trip setpoint as 6.0 barg in the narrative vs 6.5 barg in the C&E, and says it needs a design basis.
why.2: The table contrasts 2oo3 (PT-301A/B/C) in the narrative with PT-301A only (1oo1) in the C&E, and notes PT-301B/C are absent from the C&E.
why.3: The table flags the HP effects difference (narrative: stop P-301; C&E: stop P-301 + close XV-301). It also flags that ESD HS-301 is 'Not mentioned' in the narrative, which 'has no ESD section'.
why.4: It states that with auto reset, P-301 would restart as soon as level drops below the switch, causing cycling and repeated overfill risk. It requires latched trips with deliberate manual reset and a separate operator restart.
why.5: It challenges the 30 s delay as possibly exceeding the process safety time and requires justification. For the bypass, it requires authorized roles under a permit, HMI indication with alarm, time limits or shift review, logging and compensating measures, and rejects bypass from the engineering workstation.
why.6: Section 3 assigns setpoint, voting, delay, effects and reset to the C&E/SRS. It says the narrative should refer to trips by C&E row without repeating numbers, and should have those details stripped out.

why.1: The conflicts table lists the high-pressure setpoint as 6.0 barg in the narrative and 6.5 barg in the C&E, and notes that the values differ.
why.2: The table flags that the narrative specifies 2oo3 voting on PT-301A/B/C while the C&E shows only PT-301A, with B and C missing.
why.3: The table notes that the C&E closes XV-301 on high pressure but the narrative does not. It also notes that the narrative never mentions the ESD HS-301, which stops P-301 and closes XV-301 and XV-302.
why.4: The output calls automatic reset on LSHH-301 the most serious finding. It says the pump restarts by itself and causes unexpected acid transfer with nobody checking. It states that safety trips should latch and need a deliberate manual reset.
why.5: The 30 s delay is challenged against process safety time as hard to justify, with alternatives given. The blanket bypass in 6.4 must be defined per cause and access-controlled (authorization). It must also be alarmed (indication), logged, time-limited, and covered by procedure, and the ESD must never be bypassable.
why.6: The output names the C&E matrix as the single source of truth for setpoints, voting, delays, effects and resets. The narrative should reference the C&E for values without duplicating setpoints, because duplication caused the drift.

why.1: Item 1 flags the conflict: TIC-405 is labelled reverse acting but described as increasing steam on rising temperature. It names this as positive feedback and states the correct behavior: rising tray temperature means steam must decrease. It also gives corrected wording.
why.2: Item 2 flags the mismatch with the tuning sheet (0.8/12 vs 1.2/8). It recommends referencing the tuning sheet by document number rather than duplicating values in two places, which amounts to making the sheet the single source.
why.3: It gives example wording for shedding to Manual with output held at the last good value. However, the alarm is left as 'the priority to annunciate' and the return condition is left as an open question ('whether automatically or requires operator action'). It lists what must be specified rather than defining the return-to-cascade condition.
why.4: Item 4 requires TIC-405 output to track the FIC-420 setpoint or measured flow when FIC-420 is in manual. It states the purpose is to prevent windup and give a bumpless return, and it defines the restore sequence.
why.5: It does not call the LIC-411-to-reflux scheme with fixed distillate a defect. It correctly states that level up increases reflux. Item 6 only asks, as a minor item, for the rationale and the operator adjustment method to be documented, which treats the scheme as acceptable if intended.

why.1: Item 1 flags the contradiction between 'reverse acting' and 'output increases steam flow' and calls it positive feedback. It states the correct behavior (rising temperature decreases the FIC-420 setpoint) and gives corrected wording.
why.2: It flags the Kc/Ti conflict with the tuning sheet, but only recommends confirming which values are current. It does not recommend removing tuning from the narrative or making the tuning sheet the single source.
why.3: It calls the wording underspecified and lists questions (detection, manual vs hold, alarm) without defining the response. It never commits to a mode shed to manual with output held, and gives no condition for return to cascade.
why.4: Item 4 requires defining TIC-405 behavior when FIC-420 is in manual, including output tracking of the FIC-420 setpoint, bumpless return and anti-windup.
why.5: Item 5 calls the LIC-411-to-reflux scheme with fixed distillate 'workable' and only asks for confirmation of intent and limits. It does not declare the scheme a defect.

why.1: Template section 3 has a modes table with a 'Who commands start/stop' column and a speed source column. Section 5 is a start permissives table. Section 6 is a running interlocks table with per-interlock 'Latching?' and 'Reset method' columns.
why.2: Section 9 covers fail to start ('Run feedback not received within {{timer}}'), VFD fault, and drive communication loss, which is the loss of drive status and feedback. Section 10 covers instrument signal failure. Section 11 covers PLC restart and drive power loss and return.
why.3: An explicit design rule says tags, ranges, units, setpoints, delays and priorities stay in the I/O list and alarm database and are referenced by tag or alarm ID, because duplicated values will disagree. Sections 2 and 8 repeat this.
why.4: I1 (LSL-110) ramp-stops the pump, Latch: Yes, reset by operator after LSL-110 clears. I2 (LSH-120) stops the pump, Latch: Yes, reset by operator after LSH-120 clears. Both are also start permissives.
why.5: Many example statements are not testable as written. PT-1102 bad-quality behavior is left as an undecided choice. Debounce is 'short'. Batch comm loss runs 'for a set time'. At-speed is 'within a tolerance'. Minimum speed is 'enough pump flow'. Ramp vs coast is unconfirmed. Numerous [CONFIRM] placeholders leave the behavior undefined.

why.1: The template has a Modes table with columns for who commands start/stop and who commands speed. It has a Start Permissives table and a Run Interlocks table that includes a 'Reset type (auto / operator)' column for each interlock.
why.2: Section 6 calls for confirmation timeouts, and Section 9 lists failure to start, VFD fault and speed deviation. Section 13 covers wire break, bad quality and comms loss for each signal, and Section 8 covers loss of the speed reference. Section 11 asks whether auto-restart is allowed after a trip or power loss.
why.3: The template's author rule says not to type ranges, setpoints or delays and to refer to the tag instead, so the I/O list and alarm DB stay the single source of truth. Section 2 and the alarm sections repeat this.
why.4: I1 makes LSL-110 a latched trip stop that needs an operator reset once LSL-110 is clear. I2 makes LSH-120 a normal ramp-down stop that is not latched: it auto-clears and the batch system must re-command start. Section 11 and the commissioning test 'no latch' confirm this.
why.5: Several statements are too ambiguous to become FAT steps. Trip stop says the VFD 'coasts or stops per its drive configuration'. I7 says both 'Auto-clear when quality returns' and 'operator reset required', which contradict each other. The commissioning row 'Remove run feedback' expects 'Failed-to-start or run fb lost trip'. The 'clamped starting value' is never defined. Ramps are 'set on the VFD or in the PLC', and bypasses apply 'if the site permits any'.

why.1: The template requires an ID in [AREA]-[NNN] format that is never reused, plus a Verification field (I/A/D/T). Every requirement table carries an ID and a verification column. Appendix E's traceability matrix links each requirement ID to FAT, SAT and SIT tests, and Section 9 requires every Mandatory requirement to map to at least one test.
why.2: Section 4.4 makes the author get a degraded-operation ranking signed off, explicitly covering what a booster does when it can't see its reservoir. Section 5.8 requires fallback behavior and recovery for each inter-site relationship. Appendix B has a per-station 'Data timeout' and 'Fallback mode' row. PLC-001 requires each site PLC to run independently of central SCADA.
why.3: Several requirements cover this. HMI-003 visually distinguishes stale, out-of-range or substituted values. PLC-004 flags bad-quality analog signals. HIS-002 requires source timestamps. COM-005 displays and alarms comms path status. ALM-005 raises a site comms alarm. BPS03-022 shows data quality, active comms path and time since last valid update.
why.4: The How to Use guidance says: 'Describe what the system must do. Leave how to the integrator unless the utility has a standard, such as a mandated PLC platform. When you do constrain the how, record the reason in the Rationale field.'
why.5: Appendix F covers all three parts. BPS03-010 and 011 define the duty and lag start/stop levels. BPS03-014 to 017 define invalid-data detection, hold time and fallback options. BPS03-014, 016 and 019 name specific operator alarms ('RES-02 LEVEL INVALID', 'IN FALLBACK MODE', 'HIGH-HIGH PROTECTION UNAVAILABLE'). Each requirement has a verification method and observable acceptance criteria, and SIT scenarios back them up.

why.1: Section 4 sets an ID format FR-[AREA]-[NNN] with IDs never reused, and requires a verification method (T/D/I/A) plus a FAT/SAT stage for every requirement. Appendix D is a traceability matrix mapping requirement ID to test ID. The worked example carries an ID and 'Verification: T (FAT and SAT)'.
why.2: Section 7.1 (Local autonomy) and its guidance tell the author to write the loss-of-comms behaviour and safe state for every site type. Section 10.4 and the Section 10 guidance require a per-pair decision on what the pump does when the level is untrustworthy. Worked example clause (d) specifies hold-then-fallback for the booster station.
why.3: Section 6.3 defines comms health, and Section 6.4 guidance requires a heartbeat or quality/age indication on cross-site values. Section 5.5 shows the timestamp source, and Section 10.3 covers staleness. Example clause (c) defines validity by quality, age and rate of change, and clause (h) displays level age, validity status and inhibit reason on the HMI. Stale-data alarms are also required.
why.4: Section 1 guidance states that a functional spec says what the system shall do, not which product or code structure delivers it, and to name products only where the utility has a standardisation mandate. Section 5 guidance says to specify behaviours rather than vendor features. Protocols appear only as e.g. placeholders.
why.5: FR-CTL-012 defines parameterised start and stop levels (duty and assist) with hysteresis. It defines the invalid-level fallback: hold for {HOLD_TIME}, then a utility-selected fallback. It names the alarm 'RES-02 level unavailable at BPS-03' plus a high-priority alarm. Each part maps to listed acceptance tests (level sweep, blocked update, cellular path, server loss, rate injection, recovery, inhibit).

why.1: The output names the Dave vs Mike start-order conflict and adopts Dave's order. It gives an engineering basis: the fan cannot pull gas through the bags until D-704 opens, so starting the fan first gives no anti-blinding benefit. It marks the choice [TBC] and lists it as Open Item 1 for confirmation.
why.2: 'A minute or so' becomes a 60 s operator-adjustable default and 'like 6 or 7 in.' becomes a fixed 6.0 in. w.c. DP High setpoint. Neither is marked [TBC] or listed as an open item, so the confirmation marking covers only secondary values (delays, reset deadbands), not these converted approximations.
why.3: The DP High-High kiln feed stop is marked [TBC: automatic interlock or operator action], and Open Item 4 notes Dave said 'usually' and asks whether this should be an automatic interlock or an alarm with operator action.
why.4: Interlock I-1 defines the RV-702 failure response: alarm, stop kiln feed, close D-704, fan action TBC. Open Item 3 questions whether stopping F-703 is safe. Open Item 5 cites the 2019 fire and notes there is no hopper high-level switch, zero-speed switches or hopper/outlet temperature alarm in the current description.
why.5: The 450 °F alarm opens D-706 and a reset value is proposed, but the High-High trip setpoint is only [TBC]. The action if bleed air does not correct the temperature is left as '[TBC: e.g., stop kiln feed / close D-704]', so no numeric trip value or defined escalation action is given.
why.6: Section 8 ends the narrative with a numbered list of 11 open items to resolve before programming, followed by a short recommendation to review them with operations and engineering.

why.1: Section 2 flags the fan-first vs conveyor-first conflict as an open item. It proposes a default with a stated basis: fan-first runs the fan before hopper discharge is proven, a risk given the 2019 fire. It leaves the choice to the process owner (open question 1).
why.2: 'A minute or so' becomes an adjustable 60 s delay marked [CONFIRM]. 'Like 6 or 7 in.' becomes a single adjustable 6 in. w.c. setpoint marked [CONFIRM units and value]. Hysteresis is marked [TBD].
why.3: Section 4.2 picks up 'usually shut the kiln feed', proposes an automatic stop, and asks whether it should be operator-initiated instead [CONFIRM]. Open question 3 asks whether the DP > 8 feed stop is automatic or operator-initiated.
why.4: The airlock trip response is defined and a hopper high-level switch is recommended. However, the output never questions whether stopping the fan is right given the fire; it assumes stopping the fan is correct. Fire or spark detection is never raised.
why.5: It gives a 450 °F setpoint and a 425 °F example reset. No numeric trip value is given; the high-high trip is only recommended as [TBD]. There is no defined action if D-706 fails to bring the temperature down.
why.6: Section 6 ends the document with a concise numbered list of nine open questions for the supervisor.

why.1: The narrative is written in process terms: fill, fill timeout, agitation, heating and a typical sequence. However, the narrative statements are not traced to their rungs (R0–R6). Only one Part 2 item mentions 'rung 0', and the I/O table maps tags to addresses, not rungs.
why.2: Part 2 item 1 states that B3 is retained through power cycles, that rung 0 re-seals the latch, and that the tank starts filling with no operator action. It requires Run to be non-retentive and cleared on power restore, with a deliberate operator Start.
why.3: Item 4 says AGIT_HAND bypasses the low-level permissive, letting the agitator run with the tank low or empty. It notes that Hand also permits steam into a low tank. The fix is a supervised, key-switched, time-limited maintenance mode that never permits steam.
why.4: Section 4 and item 8 state that the RTO is retentive, accumulates across all top-ups and power cycles, and is reset only by Start. Item 8 warns this will eventually cause a false timeout. It proposes a per-fill-cycle timer that resets when each fill completes.
why.5: Part 1 (as-found) and Part 2 (upgrade) are clearly separated. Part 3 lists field verifications, including TEMP_LOW polarity and broken-wire state, LSH polarity, E-stop wiring, valve fail positions, drain valve, and starter feedback. [VERIFY] tags mark assumptions.

why.1: The narrative is written in process terms (filling, agitation, heating, alarm) and keeps I/O addresses. It does not trace each statement to its rung: only R6 is cited, and the fill, agitation, heating and run-latch statements have no rung references (R0–R5).
why.2: Item 1 says B3:0/0 is retained through a power cycle and the tank restarted filling without a start command. It states the upgrade must require a fresh start after power-up or a mode change, and that the FDS should state this as a requirement.
why.3: Item 2 says AGIT_HAND turns the agitator on below the low point and then permits steam into an empty tank. Items 2 and 3 propose restrictions or an alarm on hand mode and a level permissive on the steam valve.
why.4: Item 4 says the RTO accumulates across fill cycles, causing false timeouts, and resets only on START_PB. It proposes a per-fill-cycle TON that resets when the valve closes, plus a separate alarm reset.
why.5: The output has a separate 'as-found behavior' section and a separate 'Items not to carry forward' section. It also lists open questions, including what the temperature input is and its setpoint, and a caveat to verify wiring and retentive settings in the field.

why.1: Section 2 lists permissives P1–P10 in their own table, separate from the trip schedule in 6.1. The process permissives carry checkable values: TT-214 > 25 °C, PT-213 ≥ 2.2 bar held 30 s, ZT-210 ≤ minimum + 2 %, vibration below the 40 µm alarm. The rest are discrete states (FV-211 fully open, REMOTE mode, breaker ready) that a tester can verify.
why.2: Steps 1 and 2 drive the IGVs to the start position and FV-211 to 100 % open before the motor starts. Loading happens only after the 'At Speed' signal, the 60 s oil changeover and a 30 s (TBC) stabilisation period (Steps 3–5).
why.3: Pre-lube is proven by PT-213 ≥ 2.2 bar for 30 s (P3). P-212 auto-starts at 2.0 bar (TBC) if pressure falls while running, with an alarm (Step 3.3 and Table 6.1). Post-lube runs for 20 min (TBC) after shaft stop (Section 4.5).
why.4: Section 2.1 enforces a maximum of 3 starts in a rolling 60-minute window and a minimum of 20 min between hot starts, and defines a hot start. When a start is blocked, the DCS inhibits it and shows the time remaining until a start is allowed; the operator cannot bypass the inhibit.
why.5: Section 6.2: on any trip, FV-211 drives to 100 % open simultaneously with the motor trip, and the first-out is captured and displayed. Section 6.3: trips are latched, need a deliberate operator RESET, and a reset does not start the unit.
why.6: Section 5: the UCP opens FV-211 when the operating point reaches the surge control line, overriding the DCS pressure controller through a high-select. Step 5.6 and the split-range description explain how this interacts with control of the 7.0 barg header pressure.

why.1: Start permissives (4.3) are listed separately from protective trips (4.7). The numeric values are given: TT-214 >25 °C, PT-213 ≥2.5 bar, vibration below 40 µm, start limits, oil trip 1.8/1.3 bar, vibration trip 40/60 µm. The remaining permissives are discrete states a tester can check. Only the TT-214 high limits are left as [Confirm] because they are not in the design basis.
why.2: The output says the compressor starts unloaded with FV-211 fully open and the IGV at the start position. Loading begins only after the soft starter reports end of ramp. However, the delay before loading is only a 'warm-up time at no load [Confirm with vendor]' with no value, so it is not a defined delay.
why.3: Pre-lube with a pressure proof is defined: PT-213 must reach 2.5 bar within 30 s, followed by a hold. Auto start of P-212 on PT-213 below 1.8 bar while running is defined. Post-lube during rundown is only 'a post-lube time [Confirm with vendor]' with no value, so it does not run for a defined time.
why.4: Section 4.4 enforces a rolling count of 3 starts per 60 minutes and a 20-minute hot-restart timer as a start permissive, with retentive counters. The DCS displays the time remaining until the next start is allowed and the reason it is blocked.
why.5: Section 4.7 states that a trip is latched, de-energizes the motor immediately, opens FV-211, and captures and displays the first-out trip. Reset requires the cause to have cleared, the unit to be stopped, and operator acknowledgement at the DCS. Restart only happens through an operator start command subject to permissives.
why.6: Section 4.10 states that the vendor anti-surge function opens FV-211 when the operating point approaches the surge line and takes priority over the DCS pressure controller. The DCS must not command FV-211 closed or the IGV open against surge protection. The section also covers venting when header pressure is above setpoint or demand is low, and the trip on repeated surge.

why.1: X.1 assigns purge, ignition, flame supervision, SSOV control and interlock trips to the BMS. It states the DCS performs no burner safety function and that no BMS safety function depends on a DCS signal. X.10 says position proof is a BMS function and that the DCS does not shorten or bypass release permissives.
why.2: X.12 lists signals in both directions: BMS→DCS (firing, release to modulate, purge and light-off position requests, trip, state, heartbeat) and DCS→BMS (start/stop requests, reset, heartbeat). X.10 has DCS controllers tracking and holding fuel and air at the BMS purge, light-off and low-fire positions until Release to Modulate is given.
why.3: X.4 and X.7 define MIN/MAX cross-limit equations with margins. Air leads fuel on increase and fuel leads air on decrease, explicitly to prevent a fuel-rich condition.
why.4: X.8 clamps K_trim to 0.90–1.10 and rate-limits it. Trim is enabled only when AT-313 quality is good and the reading is within the 0.5–12% plausibility range. Otherwise K_trim ramps to 1.00 with an analyzer-fault alarm.
why.5: X.10 says that on a trip FV-311 is forced closed immediately and all controllers go to tracking to prevent windup. On release, PIC-310 is initialized to low-fire demand for bumpless transfer and then ramps at the rate limit, so modulation does not resume from stale outputs.

why.1: Section 1 assigns purge, light-off, flame supervision, safety shutoff valves and all trips/MFT to the vendor BMS. It states the DCS performs no safety function, cannot open safety shutoff valves or override a BMS trip, and that the BMS can always override DCS outputs. Section 4.3 adds that the DCS does not report proof on the BMS's behalf.
why.2: Section 4.2 lists hardwired signals in both directions: BMS→DCS (purge, low-fire hold required, flame proven, modulation released, MFT, purge-air request) and DCS→BMS (start/stop, fan ready, watchdog, trip request). Sections 2 and 4.3 state the DCS holds fan, damper and FV-311 at BMS-required purge and light-off positions until the BMS releases modulation.
why.3: Section 3.2 gives max/min cross-limit equations on measured flows. It states explicitly that air leads on load increases and fuel leads on decreases, so the mixture stays lean through transients.
why.4: Section 3.5 limits trim to ±[10%] and prevents it from going below the minimum excess air curve. It enables trim only when AT-313 is healthy, and on analyzer failure or calibration the trim freezes, ramps to zero over [2 min] and alarms. Section 3.6 adds range and deviation quality checks on AT-313.
why.5: Section 4.3 says that on MFT the DCS sets the master to light-off demand and tracks. Section 2 says controllers track their output in all non-modulating modes and transitions are bumpless, so the handover starts from the actual light-off position. Restart requires purge and BMS release.

why.1: Hold condition H1 stops the feed when SI-501 speed is below AGIT_MIN_SPEED or A-501 is not running, so speed is checked, not just the run signal. H3 and H4 stop it on high reaction temperature (85 °C proposed and the 88 °C alarm). H5 stops it when TV-506A demand is at or above COOL_MARGIN_HI (90%) for a set time.
why.2: Section 7.2 says restart is operator-initiated only and no automatic restart is permitted. Restart requires accumulation below ACCUM_RESTART_LIM, all start permissives met, supervisor authorization for an H1 agitator hold, and a ramped return to rate. Section 7.1 also forbids automatic agitator restart.
why.3: Section 6.3 defines a heat-balance calculation of accumulated monomer (feed integral minus Q_rxn/ΔH_r) with a hold at ACCUM_HOLD_LIM. It adds secondary signatures: Tr−Tj below EXO_MIN_DT (H8), steam valve opening (H6) and low reaction temperature (H2). The action is an automatic Hold with the feed closed. Step 3 adds initiation confirmation that goes to Hold on timeout.
why.4: Section 7 covers all four states. Holding sets FIC-510 SP to 0 in Manual at 0%, closes and confirms XV-510, and leaves temperature control at 80 °C unchanged. Restart opens XV-510 and ramps the rate back up. Stop ramps to 0, closes XV-510 and leaves temperature control and agitation running. Abort closes XV-510 immediately, drives FIC-510 to 0% and requests maximum cooling (TV-506A open, TV-506B closed).
why.5: Step 5 ends the feed when the totalizer reaches FEED_TOTAL_SP minus a pre-close allowance, and H10 catches overfeed. Section 6.2 alarms when feed duration exceeds the expected FEED_TOTAL_SP/FEED_RATE_SP plus a TBD percentage.
why.6: Section 1 states the SIS is independent and that the phase does not depend on it. The phase uses its own lower limits (85/88 °C) and does not duplicate the 95 °C trip. It only follows an SIS trip to a safe state, and clearing Abort never resets the SIS.

why.1: Feed stops on SI-501 speed below minimum and on high temperature (cutback at about 85 C, stop at the 88 C alarm). There is no rule to stop feed on loss of cooling margin, such as TV-506A near full open. Cooling valve position is used only as a heat-release proxy.
why.2: After agitation loss, the output says to resume only after speed is restored and an operator reviews the accumulation estimate. On Restart it requires repeating the initiation feed and reaction confirmation. Resumption after an accumulation-type hold is stated to be not automatic.
why.3: Defines detection through a reactor/jacket heat balance, or a cooling-demand proxy (TV-506A position and TIC-506 output) compared against the expected heat release. Also uses a low-temperature check. The action is to stop the feed and go to Hold (reason: accumulation).
why.4: The ISA-88 state table covers Holding/Held, Restarting, Stopping and Aborting. It gives FIC-510 at 0%, the block valve closed, TV-506B closed, and TIC-505/506 kept in cascade at 80 C. It also states agitator behavior.
why.5: Completion is the totalizer reaching the recipe quantity, but there is no rule for a feed that takes much longer than expected. There is no maximum feed time or elapsed-time deviation. The only time limit is the hold duration on restart.
why.6: States that the 95 C trip is a separate SIS function that acts independently and that the phase only monitors for it. It also says the phase logic must not be the only protection.

why.1: Section 4.2 sets a BW_IN_PROGRESS interlock that allows one filter at a time. It defines a FIFO queue and gives a priority order for simultaneous requests: turbidity > headloss > operator > run time.
why.2: Section 5 redistributes flow as Plant flow ÷ N_online, giving 416.7 m³/h each on 3 filters, with a 5 min ramp. Section 4.2 holds the request and raises an alarm if plant flow ÷ 3 would exceed the max filtration rate.
why.3: Steps state 'confirm closed/open' for the valves. Section 7 defines a failure to reach position within travel time + 10 s as HOLD with an alarm naming the valve. Every step has a step timeout leading to HOLD.
why.4: HOLD freezes outputs and pauses timers. From HOLD the operator can Resume, Skip Step or Abort. ABORT lists the safe valve and equipment states: B-1 stopped, FV-n04 closed, FCV-n03 closed and pump stopped, FV-n06/FCV-n02 closed, drain open 2 min then closed, influent closed. The filter goes Out of Service and is not re-queued. After a power failure there is no automatic resume and the operator restarts or releases the filter.
why.5: Step S8: when 30 min elapses with turbidity ≥ 0.1 NTU, the alarm 'FTW turbidity not achieved' is raised, FV-n06 and FV-n01 close, and the filter goes to Standby – Operator Release Required rather than returning to service automatically.
why.6: Clearwell ≥ 3.0 m is a start permissive (4.3). A level below 2.5 m during the wash triggers ABORT with a low-low alarm. If the duty pump fails or trips, the standby pump starts automatically, and ABORT follows if both pumps fail.

why.1: The permissives state 'Only one filter may be backwashed at a time' and block a start while another filter is in backwash, filter-to-waste or ripening. A queue priority is defined: turbidity, then headloss, then run time, then operator request, with the oldest request first within a priority.
why.2: Step 1 ramps the other three filters to take 30 ML/d at 10 ML/d each. A MinOnline / maximum filtration rate permissive blocks a wash if the remaining filters would exceed the maximum rate, and there is an abort if another filter trips.
why.3: The output states 'a step advances only on proven valve position'. The fault table gives a 30 s valve fail-to-open/close timeout with safe stop, alarm and filter lockout.
why.4: Holds and aborts are defined. Clearwell low-low stops the pump and blower, closes the water valve, holds the filter in 'wash incomplete' and resumes after the level recovers. An operator abort leaves the filter isolated and drained. A safe-stop order is given (blower, water ramp, pump, valves). Other faults lock out the filter until acknowledged, so the conditions for resuming are stated, although the resume entry point is only thinly described.
why.5: The chosen default on a 30 min filter-to-waste timeout raises a high-priority alarm and holds the filter out of service pending operator action. Automatic return is mentioned only as a configurable alternative.
why.6: A clearwell level above 3.0 m is a start permissive. A clearwell abort below 2.5 m stops the wash safely. P-BW1/P-BW2 failover is defined: swap to standby if the duty pump fails to prove running within 15 s or trips, hold the timer, retry once, and safe stop if both pumps fail.

why.1: The start sequence in §5 runs CV-3, CR-1, CV-2, CV-1, VF-1 in that order. Each conveyor must show its zero-speed switch healthy within 8 s before the next step, or the sequence aborts. CR-1 has no zero-speed switch, so it is proven by run feedback and its motor current dropping after inrush.
why.2: Normal stop (§6.2) stops VF-1 first, then CV-1, CV-2, CR-1 and CV-3 in flow order. §6.1 gives each conveyor its own run-out timer (T_RO1/2/3, 20–45 s, set from the measured empty-belt time) and gives CR-1 a current-based run-out.
why.3: Principle 3 and §7 say a trip stops the affected unit and everything upstream immediately, while downstream units keep running. The §7.4 cascade table spells this out for every unit.
why.4: §1 and §7.1 say pull-cords are hardwired into a safety circuit that removes motor power independently of the PLC, and the PLC only monitors them. §2 and §8 require a local reset at the switch plus a safety relay reset, neither possible from the HMI.
why.5: §7.2 uses the CR-1 CT with defined thresholds below the trip levels: above 180 A for 3 s holds or reduces the VF-1 rate, and above 200 A for 5 s stops VF-1 with auto-resume below 150 A. The overload trip is set at 231 A and the stall trip at 315 A.
why.6: §4 requires a non-bypassable 10 s horn and beacon before each conveyor starts, and voids the warning if the start is delayed. §5 applies it to every conveyor in the start sequence, and §6.4 and §8 apply the full 10 s warning to every stopped conveyor on restart after a stop, trip or E-stop.

why.1: Section 4 starts CV-3, then CR-1, CV-2, CV-1 and VF-1, each only after the previous item is proven. The conveyors are proven by their ZS within a start-up timer. CR-1 has no ZS in the task, so it is proven by its running current, which is reasonable.
why.2: Section 6 stops VF-1 first, then CV-1, CV-2, CR-1 and CV-3. It sets run-out times T1, T2 and T3 per conveyor within 20-45 s, plus a crusher clearing time, so the belts empty.
why.3: Section 2 and sections 5.1-5.6 state that a trip stops the tripped item and everything upstream while downstream items run out. A summary table gives the outcome for each case, and the pull-cord exception is justified.
why.4: The output requires a local reset of the pull-cords and an HMI acknowledgement. It never says the pull-cords act directly on the motor circuits independent of the PLC, or that the PLC only monitors them. The hardwired path is mentioned only for the control room stop button.
why.5: CR-1 current is used only for alarms (110% FLC, 231 A) and trips (125% FLC, about 262 A). Nothing reduces or stops the VF-1 feed before the overload trip is reached.
why.6: Section 4 runs the 10 s warning before any equipment moves. Sections 5.3 and 7 require a normal start with the full 10 s warning before any restart after a trip.

why.1: Problem 1 flags that LAHH-201 (90%) is below LAH-201 (93%). The corrected section restores the order: LAH at 85%, then LAHH at 88%, then BPCS action at 90%, then SIS trip at 93%.
why.2: Problems 2 and 4 address the PLC closure at 92% and the 'independent' LSHH at 95%. The output defines them as two distinct layers: BPCS action in 4.3.3 and an independent SIS in 4.3.4 with its own sensor and logic solver. It states the required ordering (alarm, then BPCS, then SIS, then overfill) and resolves the conflicting values with ordered setpoints.
why.3: Problem 3 explicitly states that closing XV-201 deadheads the fixed-speed PD pump P-201. Corrected 4.3.3 requires stopping P-201, confirming it has stopped, then closing XV-201, and forbids closing the valve while the pump runs. The SIS trips the pump at the motor starter. Surge and relief checks are required, and 4.3.7 requires notifying the pipeline operator.
why.4: Problem 5 flags the HMI bypass as unsafe and explains why the level-based auto-reset is backwards. Corrected 4.3.5 requires a work permit plus key switch or password-controlled supervisor authorization, continuous HMI alarm, logging, and automatic removal after a set number of hours. It also has the SIS itself block pump start and valve opening during a bypass. The bypass hardware is not explicitly stated to sit outside the BPCS, but SIS-side enforcement keeps the bypass independent of the BPCS.
why.5: Corrected 4.3.2 defines LT-201 failure or bad-quality behavior: a priority alarm, then the operator stops the receipt until level is confirmed by manual gauging. Frozen values are not explicitly mentioned. Problem 7 replaces 'should' with 'shall'. Corrected 4.3.6 replaces 'level is OK' with defined reset conditions: LT-201 below a numeric MW level (e.g. 85%), LSHH cleared, and the cause reviewed. Restart is a separate, deliberate operator action.

why.1: Issue 1 flags that LAH at 93% sits above LAHH at 90%. The corrected table orders them LAH 90%, LAHH 92%, BPCS trip 93%, LSHH 95%.
why.2: Issue 1 lists the PLC close at 92% and the LSHH at 95% as two distinct actions. The correction defines them as separate layers: a BPCS trip at 93% from LT-201, and an independent LSHH trip at 95% through an SIS or independent logic solver. Issue 7 explains the independence requirement, so the two-layer design is justified.
why.3: Issue 2 states that closing XV-201 against the fixed-speed PD pump with no recirculation line deadheads it. It requires both trips to stop P-201, sets the order (P-201 stopped before or with XV-201 closing), and bases XV-201 closure time on a pipeline surge check.
why.4: Issue 3 states that the HMI bypass is not independent and that a level-based reset may never clear. The correction requires supervisor key authorization, a 30-minute time-out, annunciation and logging, and a hardwired switch kept independent of the BPCS.
why.5: 4.3.3 trips on bad LT-201 signal quality, and Issue 8 raises loss of signal and power. Frozen value is not named, but bad-signal failure behavior is defined. 'Should' is replaced with 'shall' throughout. 'Level is OK' is replaced with a latched trip and a manual reset allowed only below 85% with LSHH clear.

why.1: Item G says a 75°F dry-bulb changeover in Houston admits very humid air (about 70°F dewpoint) and raises latent load. It cites a 65°F fixed dry-bulb limit for zone 2A and recommends fixed or differential enthalpy.
why.2: Item J flags the missing deadband and the risk of chatter or hunting. It never says the split-range description fails to state valve direction (open or closed) at each end of the signal, which is half of this expectation.
why.3: Item E flags the automatic restart as atypical and says most specs require manual reset to prevent short-cycling. It states that on a trip the heating valve should be driven 100% open.
why.4: Item D says shutdown should be hardwired to the fan starter or VFD safety circuit, not dependent on BAS logic, citing IMC 606 and NFPA 90A. It says restart should require the detector to be reset or cleared at the fire alarm panel, not just an alarm acknowledgment at the workstation.
why.5: Item F rejects 'last position' and gives defined fail positions: HV-3 fail open for freeze protection, CV-3 fail closed (or per engineer), and the OA damper spring-return fail closed. Reasons are given for HV-3 and implied for the isolation dampers.

why.1: Item 5 says a 75 F dry-bulb limit is wrong for humid Houston air (90%+ RH, coil load, condensation and mold). It proposes an enthalpy or dewpoint lockout, and item 6 suggests basing the enable on a lower OA temperature.
why.2: Item 10 flags the missing deadband at the 50% crossover, hunting, and the need for interlocks so the valves don't fight. It never says the split-range description fails to state valve direction (open/closed) at each end of the output range, so part of the expectation is not addressed.
why.3: Item 2 flags the auto-restart at 40 F (short-cycling, pulling in cold air) and says freezestats are normally hardwired and manual reset. It requires HV-3 to be driven fully open with the hot water pump started on a freeze condition.
why.4: Item 1 says stopping the fan through the BAS is a software path. It cites NFPA 90A/IMC requiring a hardwired interlock with the BAS as monitoring only, and says restart must be a manual reset at the detector or fire alarm panel, not a BAS acknowledgement.
why.5: Item 3 rejects 'last position' as unacceptable for coil protection. It specifies HV-3 fail open, OA damper fail closed (spring return) and CV-3 fail closed, and also covers power-restore behavior.

why.1: Finding 11 says 'any circuit selected' can send hot caustic toward live product. Section 7.2.2 requires the circuit to be out of production (S-1 level empty with product valves proven closed; HTST-1 in CIP mode). It also requires mix-proof valve position feedback confirmed and segregating valves proven closed before start.
why.2: Section 7.2.1 says the step timer counts only while TT-501 is at or above the recipe minimum and CT-501 is inside the concentration window, with flow and P-502 also required. The timer holds on deviation and resets after [60 s] out of spec.
why.3: 'Heated to temperature' becomes per-circuit numeric caustic return temperatures measured on TT-501 (e.g. ≥70 °C and ≥75–80 °C). 'Run until clean' becomes CT-501 at or below a final rinse conductivity setpoint (potable water conductivity plus margin), held for [60 s] with a minimum time.
why.4: Section 7.2.4 handles P-502 failure by immediately stopping P-501, closing the supply valve, holding the timer and raising a high-priority alarm. For FT-501 below minimum flow it holds the timer, alarms, then scavenges and pauses. This replaces 'operator should check'.
why.5: Steps 2–5 in the table route the return to drain until CT-501 reaches the arrival setpoint, then to tank recovery. During push-out the return goes to the tank until CT-501 falls to the recovery cut-off, then to drain. Drain/scavenge periods are also added between phases.

why.1: Item 9 calls 'any circuit selected on the HMI' unsafe. The start permissives (7.2.2) require that the circuit is not in production and holds no product, that S-1 level is below a limit, and that mix-proof valve positions are confirmed by feedback before chemicals are introduced. The other circuit must also be isolated.
why.2: Timers pause only while FT-501 is below minimum or return temperature is below setpoint. Return conductivity is used only as an end criterion (caustic conductivity band), not as a condition for counting wash time. There is no pause or extension when conductivity drops.
why.3: 'Heated to temperature' becomes a TT-501 return setpoint of [75 °C] at which the timer starts. 'Until clean' becomes CT-501 ≤ [limit] for [60 s] continuous, plus a minimum time. Both are defined numeric criteria held as recipe parameters.
why.4: 7.2.5 defines the P-502 fault response: P-501 stops, heating is disabled, the sequence holds, a high-priority alarm is raised, and it aborts on timeout. 7.2.3 defines FT-501 low flow beyond [30 s]: the step holds, an alarm is raised and timers pause. This replaces 'operator should check'.
why.5: The step table routes chemical returns back to the caustic and acid tanks and rinse water to drain. Rinse steps end on CT-501 ≤ limit, and the text states that interface cuts between water and chemical are based on CT-501. Valve transitions wait for feedback. Recovery versus drain is also raised as an open question.
